title: She Fought for Women's Rights and Was Executed for Treason
dek: Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist claims, but for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.
why: To understand women's political situation and individual fate during the French Revolution. History buffs and those interested in women's issues will find it compelling.
who: Anyone interested in the French Revolution, women's history, and women's writing during the Enlightenment, especially readers who want details of women's political participation beyond the textbook.
skip: The first four-plus minutes, covering her early life with its many ambiguities, can be fast-forwarded; the core content begins in the middle.

points.h: The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man
points.body: Olympe de Gouges is most famous for her 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she switched to the feminine form citoyenne, which looks completely different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this one pamphlet, and her death sentence was not for calling for women's rights.

points.h: Biographical truth is mixed with novelistic invention
points.body: De Gouges's first English biography, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, drew heavily on her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but the book is highly fictional. Its protagonist is widely considered a stand-in for herself, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This parentage remains unconfirmed to this day.

points.h: The Comédie-Française suppressed a woman playwright
points.body: Zamore and Mirza was written and submitted anonymously in 1784, accepted the following year but long delayed in production. When de Gouges kept pressing, the theater actually revoked her admission rights and applied to have her arrested. Between 1761 and 1789, the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only writer treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her standing.

points.h: Slavery became the first abolitionist play
points.body: In 1789 the play finally opened, but the setting moved from the East Indies to the Caribbean, the characters changed from Asians to Africans, and the title became Slavery of the Blacks. It is often regarded as France's first play to explicitly support abolition and to tell the story from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy colonists hired hecklers to disrupt it, and actors refused to blacken their skin for the roles.

points.h: The article rewrites all 17 articles one by one
points.body: The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted rights to citizens but excluded women, and the 1791 constitution restricted the vote to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the 17-article format and rewrote each one. For example, where the original's Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, she added that a mother has the right to publicly declare the father of her child. The whole document was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, encouraging her to advance women's rights.

points.h: Defending Louis XVI became ammunition against her
points.body: Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed a constitutional monarchy suited France best, with the king as a symbol rather than a power. In 1792, during Louis XVI's treason trial, she volunteered to defend him, arguing that since the monarchy had been abolished, the republic could not try a former king for acts committed while he reigned. Her logic was called strained, the king was executed anyway, and she herself was seen as a royalist.

points.h: Her federalist proposal led to arrest
points.body: In July 1793, de Gouges suggested that France's provinces govern themselves rather than form a unified republic, which was seen as a direct provocation. She underestimated the fierce political atmosphere of the Terror, voluntarily bringing investigators to her office, thinking her works would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Saved was used as evidence against her for sympathizing with Marie Antoinette. She was ultimately executed for opposing the republican constitution.

terms.def: The French masculine noun for a male citizen. De Gouges used citoyenne, its feminine form.
